title: The Lantern Ledger
subtitle: Lanternweald — sixth expansion pass
content:
The new ledger had no columns for loyalty.

That was Neri's first rule.

We sat at a long table in Moonroot Archive, comparing the surviving pages of the old arrival book with a clean blank volume. The old book had been designed for people who believed that crossing into Lanternweald created a debt. It recorded names, expected return dates, assigned keepers, and—in several places—marks that might have indicated whether someone had been permitted to leave.

Some of those marks made my skin crawl.

"Are we keeping any of this?" I asked.

Neri touched the cover.

"We need to preserve the original as evidence. We do not need to make a new version of its authority."

Severus, working at the next desk, looked up.

"An excellent distinction."

Orin had prepared a proposed format for the public record. It listed structural events, maintenance decisions, funding approvals, and testimony categories. Personal travel details would be kept only when someone requested help and only for as long as the service required. Romantic relationships were not part of the civic record.

The reading table had been lowered after Edda watched three visitors struggle to reach its writing surface. One leg was still propped on a wedge of scrap wood. Whenever Maui leaned forward, the ink bottle rattled.

"Stop attacking the furniture," Severus said.

"I'm reading," Maui replied.

"Then your technique requires revision."

Maui stepped away with theatrical dignity. "Observe. Flawless reading posture."

Orin pressed the table's corner. It shifted anyway.

"The repair order is still open," they said. "The record isn't public in any useful sense if half the people who need it can't write on the table."

A charcoal line on the floor marked a turning space. Someone had moved the chair across it.

I moved the chair back and fetched the order. One line specified the table leg, another a lamp that shone directly into a reader's eyes. Neither would reveal the erased keeper's name, but both mattered to the person who wanted to read the record.

Maui raised his hook. "I can hold the table steady all day."

"An admirable proposal," Severus said, "if the archive intends to employ you as permanent furniture."

"Very handsome furniture."

"We have a maintenance budget," Orin said. "We will use it."

I noted the temporary assistance arrangement until the repair could be tested. Neri approved the sign. Severus returned to his evidence list. Maui put down his hook, apparently devastated that a perfectly good heroic job had been assigned to a carpenter.

"Nobody appreciates an architectural legend," he muttered.

"Nobody wants to write on one," I said.

I wanted to hug the person who'd written that sentence.

Instead I told Orin it was good work.

They looked delighted.

The hardest part was the blank line.

It belonged to the erased signature from the Closed Bells ledger. The investigation had documented the order, the materials, the closure, and Neri's witness account of a person denied departure. But the name on the original page was gone, and none of the surviving evidence established it with sufficient confidence.

Avel, the councilor who had demanded a name before, came to review the draft.

"You're leaving the blank?" he asked.

"Yes," Neri said.

"People will think you're protecting someone."

"Then the note beside it should explain exactly why it's blank," Severus answered.

I turned the page around so Avel could read it.

*Signature removed from the surviving document. Identity unverified. The harm caused by the closure is documented independently. Additional evidence may be submitted without mandatory public disclosure.*

Avel read it twice.

He looked tired.

"I want someone to answer for what happened."

"So do I," I said. "That doesn't give us permission to choose a person because the empty space makes us angry."

He sat down.

For a moment I thought he might begin another argument. Instead he asked to see the evidence list.

We showed him the invoices, tide charts, witness summary, and the notes explaining what each could and could not prove. We also showed him the emergency policy changes already enacted because of the investigation: voluntary departure routes, clear access to the upper hall, no public lists of destinations, and reviewable decisions during closures.

He studied them.

"This is more than a blank," he said finally.

"Yes," Neri answered. "It is the work around it."

Before we released the draft, Orin caught a problem in the access rules.

"A public correction," they said, tracing the margin, "might reproduce somebody's private statement if we're not careful. Suppose a person gives us an account in confidence and later asks us to correct the date. Do we announce the whole account to prove we fixed it?"

Neri looked at the page.

"No."

"Then the correction procedure needs two paths," Orin said. "One for public evidence and one for confidential testimony."

Severus put down his pen.

"That is not a minor adjustment."

Orin's face fell.

"It's a necessary one," he continued. "My objection is to how easily we could have overlooked it."

We drew two parallel columns. Public documents could receive a dated correction note that cited the original. Confidential statements would be reviewed with their contributor, with only an appropriately limited public summary when the contributor agreed. Emergency information could be used for safety without turning a frightened traveler's identity into festival gossip.

A visitor from Tideglass arrived with a damaged invoice. They wanted to know whether the bill had been paid before the old closure, but they did not want their family's name displayed.

"Can you check without publishing it?" they asked.

Neri explained the process we'd just written.

"Good," the visitor said. "Then I'd like you to look."

The transaction was small, one box of hinges. It did not name the missing keeper or resolve the Closed Bells. Orin recorded what it did establish and carefully marked the rest unknown.

I felt a strange relief. The blank signature wasn't the only place where uncertainty mattered. Every small record needed a way for people to challenge it without surrendering the privacy the new rules were meant to protect.

When the visitor left, Severus looked at Orin.

"You have improved the procedure."

Orin smiled.

"By finding a mistake?"

"That is generally how improvement begins," he said.

Maui, carrying the empty paper wrapping from the printer, leaned in.

"You need an expert in mistakes? Lucky day. I've made some legendary ones. None came with such spectacularly boring handwriting, but I can adapt."

"Please refrain," Severus answered.

I laughed, and Neri added the correction policy to the first page where every reader could see it.

The ledger was opened to public review the following week.

People came with questions, corrections, and memories. Some brought documents; others asked whether they could give testimony privately. One person declined to leave a name and was told that was their choice. Another requested a copy of the revised emergency rules for a homeworld council dealing with flood evacuations.

Neri gave them the public version.

Nobody received keys to private files merely because they were curious.

Maui came in during the second afternoon, carrying a parcel of paper from the printer. He set it on the table and looked at the ledger.

"A ledger without a column for the biggest hero in the room?" he asked, setting down the parcel. "I demand a recount."

"There isn't a contest," Neri said.

"Then why am I losing?"

Mini Maui drew an enormous star on his chest, struck it out, and pointed to the unfilled private record. For a moment Maui's expression turned thoughtful.

"People used to write down who belonged to whom?" he asked.

"Who had authority to send travelers away or keep them here," Neri said.

His jaw tightened. He could joke about a competition, but the idea of somebody being trapped by a mark in a book seemed to anger him in a way the missing line never had.

"All right," he said, a little too loudly. "New rule. If somebody wants to go, you let them go. If they want to come back, you ask whether they want company. If they want bread—"

"Mara handles bread," I interrupted.

"She does. Very well. The great Maui merely delivers it."

He grinned again, but he didn't try to fill the blank line. It wasn't his story to complete.

"That's the famous blank line?"

"Yes," I said.

He leaned closer.

"Looks smaller than I imagined."

"Most important things do."

He grinned.

Severus made a disapproving noise.

"Please do not encourage him."

I laughed.

Later, when the visitors had gone, I found Neri standing alone by the display case.

"How are you?" I asked.

They considered.

"Less certain than I once was. More responsible, perhaps."

"That sounds exhausting."

"It is."

They smiled faintly.

"I thought telling the truth would finally let me stop carrying it."

"Did it?"

"No. But now other people can help carry the work."

I looked at the new ledger.

The old book would remain in the archive, preserved with its flaws. The new one would be revised when evidence changed or policies failed. Its pages were numbered, its handling rules public, and its blank lines explained instead of quietly filled by whoever held the pen.

Maui waited for me at the arch.

"Ready to go home?" he asked.

"In a minute."

I wrote one final note in the green notebook.

*Accountability is not a perfect story. It is a record that lets other people ask questions tomorrow.*

I closed it.

Then I took Maui's hand and went through the open passage toward the square, where the lanterns were coming on one by one.

The next day a young visitor came back with a correction.

Their family's crossing had been entered as a departure at dusk, but the ferry hadn't sailed until the following morning. The public map used that time to estimate the last safe crossing, and the error made the old route look more reliable than it was.

Orin found the source note.

"You're right," they said. "The time was copied from the departure request, not the actual tide record."

Neri asked whether the visitor wanted to attach a private statement or have the correction attributed anonymously.

"Anonymous, please."

"Then that's what we'll do."

The public page received a dated correction and a link to the weather record. Nobody wrote the visitor's name beside it. The next ferry schedule carried the revised time.

I watched the process with a feeling I couldn't quite name. We had spent so much time worrying about a missing historical signature that I'd forgotten how much a smaller error could matter to somebody trying to get home.

Severus came to inspect the update. He checked the reference, nodded once, and said, "A better ledger is one that can be corrected without a trial."

Orin grinned.

Maui leaned over my shoulder.

"And one that doesn't expect me to understand every column?"

"That may be asking too much," I said.

He laughed.

There were ordinary lives on both sides of every line we kept. That was what the new book had to remember.

The ledger stayed where it belonged.

Not beneath a crown.

On a table that could be reached.
